composition: Base element Fe; the alloy was designed as a Fe-35Mn-6Al low-density steel with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-6Al-1C-0.1Nb-0.1V-1Mo-1W (wt%) as given in the paper's materials section. Wet-chemical analysis of the solution-treated 6Al bulk gives (wt%): Mn 35.14, Al 5.97, C 0.095, Nb 0.11, V 0.10, Mo 1.24, W 0.95, Fe balance, confirming the measured Al level matches the nominal 6 wt% target. EPMA of the individual phases shows Al partitions preferentially into ferrite: the austenite (6Al_γ) contains Mn 35.92, Al 5.88, C 0.098, Nb 0.09, V 0.09, Mo 1.12, W 0.86, whereas the ferrite (6Al_α) contains Mn 32.44, Al 6.83, Nb 0.09, V 0.18, Mo 1.54 and W 1.63 with C below detection. The design intent is a lightweight Fe-Mn-Al-C steel in which Al lowers density (measured density 7.18 g cm⁻³ for 6Al, versus 7.42 and 6.99 g cm⁻³ for 4Al and 8Al) and acts as a ferrite stabiliser to tune the austenite/ferrite balance.
conclusions: The 6Al steel is the austenite-matrix duplex lightweight steel of the Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C series, positioned between the single-phase austenitic 4Al steel and the ferrite-based duplex 8Al/10Al steels; its microstructure evolves with increasing Al from single-phase austenite (4Al) to austenite-matrix duplex (6Al) and then ferrite-matrix duplex (8Al, 10Al), with DO3 ordered domains coexisting inside both B2 domains and the ferrite and growing progressively with Al content. Relative to the 4Al austenitic steel, the 6Al steel gives a small gain in strength (yield strength 251 versus 239 MPa; ultimate tensile strength 589 versus 552 MPa) at essentially unchanged ductility (uniform elongation 37.6 % versus 38.5 %; total elongation 51.6 % versus 52.0 %). The paper's broader conclusion is that the synergistic operation of edge-dislocation activity and the dynamic slip band refinement (DSBR) effect in a ferrite matrix underlies the superior strength-ductility balance of the 8Al ferrite-based duplex lightweight steel (455 MPa yield strength, 740 MPa tensile strength, 31.0 % uniform elongation), whereas the 10Al steel becomes brittle (about 4.6 % total elongation) owing to coarsening of DO3 domains and formation of 18R martensite. The study thereby reveals a new ductility-enhancing mechanism for ferrite + austenite duplex steels and offers a route for designing BCC-based low-density steels with high strength and high ductility.
mechanisms: Al as a ferrite stabiliser controls the phase balance: raising Al from 4 wt% to 6 wt% changes the microstructure from single-phase austenite (4Al) to an austenite-matrix duplex structure (6Al, 3.0 % α / 97.0 % γ), with the minority ferrite grains nucleating mainly at austenite grain boundaries; Al is preferentially partitioned into the ferrite (6Al_α = 6.83 wt% Al versus 6Al_γ = 5.88 wt% Al).

During oil quenching, spinodal decomposition of Al and C in the austenite produces nanoscale concentration fluctuations, evidenced by satellite diffraction spots near the γ reflections in [100]γ SADPs and by very weak {110} ordered spots, which correspond to L1_2-type short-range ordered domains coherent within the austenite matrix.

Within the minority ferrite, B2 and DO3 ordered domains develop: the relative intensities of the (1-11)_DO3 and (002)_DO3 dark-field images show that DO3 ordered domains coexist inside both the B2 domains and the ferrite matrix, with a maximum DO3 domain size of about 2.0 nm in the 6Al steel.

Phase-specific deformation: in the duplex structure the austenite deforms by dislocation cell blocks and dense dislocation bands regardless of Al content (the behaviour common to low-carbon/low-aluminium lightweight steels), whereas the ferrite deforms by pronounced planar slip that generates straight parallel slip bands.

The planar slip of ferrite (unusual for BCC) is attributed to the interaction between gliding dislocations and the ordered B2/DO3 structures: dislocations must travel in pairs to shear the ordered domains, leaving anti-phase boundaries behind, which keeps slip confined to planar bands; the 6Al ferrite shows less pronounced planar slip than 8Al ferrite, indicating that increasing Al promotes planar slip of ferrite dislocations.

Al raises the stacking-fault energy of the austenite (51.25 → 62.64 → 68.47 mJ m⁻² for 4Al → 6Al → 8Al at 23 °C), consistent with the high-SFE austenite deforming by planar glide of dislocations rather than by twinning or martensitic transformation in the low-Al members of the series.

Because the ferrite is markedly harder than the austenite, it acts as the strengthening phase of the duplex structure; the surrounding softer austenite and the γ/α interfaces govern how stress is partitioned and accommodated between the two phases (the detailed interface stress-partitioning and edge-dislocation mechanism of the paper is demonstrated on the 8Al steel rather than on 6Al).
microstructure: In the solution-treated state the 6Al steel is an austenite-based duplex lightweight steel with quasi-equiaxed grains: EBSD phase mapping shows a red (austenite) matrix with a sparse minority of blue (ferrite) grains located mostly at the austenite grain boundaries, and the austenite grains contain numerous annealing twin boundaries. XRD gives the phase constitution as 3.0 % α (ferrite, BCC) / 97.0 % γ (austenite, FCC) by mass, so it is the austenite-matrix duplex member of the Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C series (4Al single austenite → 6Al austenite-matrix duplex → 8Al/10Al ferrite-based duplex). [100]γ selected-area diffraction patterns show satellite spots near the γ reflections plus very weak {110} ordered spots indexed as L1_2-type short-range order; the satellites arise from Al and C concentration fluctuations, i.e. spinodal decomposition during quenching. [110]α // [110]_DO3 ferrite patterns show distinct 1-11_DO3, 002_DO3 and 001_B2 superlattice reflections, and paired DO3 dark-field images indicate that DO3 ordered domains coexist within both the B2 ordered domains and the ferrite matrix; the maximum DO3 ordered domain size in 6Al is estimated from TEM dark-field to be about 2.0 nm, the smallest of the three ferrite-bearing steels (8Al ≈ 2.1 nm, 10Al ≈ 19 nm). After tensile deformation the austenite is characterized by dislocation cell blocks and dense, aligned dislocation bands, while the ferrite shows pronounced planar slip forming straight parallel slip bands — a deformation mode described as rare in BCC structures; the planar slip in 6Al ferrite is less pronounced than in 8Al ferrite.
processing: Ingots were prepared by vacuum induction melting under a high-purity Ar atmosphere with the nominal composition above. The as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1150 °C for 4 h and then hot-forged into rods of 16.5 mm diameter. The forged bars were solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by oil quenching, which produces a microstructure with nearly equiaxed grains; this terminal solution treatment defines the "6Al" sample and is shared by all four designed steels (4Al, 6Al, 8Al, 10Al). Tensile specimens (5 mm diameter, 25 mm gauge length) were machined from the quenched rods with the tensile axis parallel to the rod axis; the paper notes the specimens were machined from quenched rods.
properties: Room-temperature tensile properties of the solution-treated 6Al steel, measured parallel to the rod axis at a strain rate of 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ on standard cylindrical specimens (5 mm diameter, 25 mm gauge length; at least three specimens tested to fracture): yield strength 251 ± 3 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 589 ± 18 MPa, uniform elongation 37.6 ± 0.9 %, total elongation 51.6 ± 1.5 %. The engineering and true stress-strain curves (Fig. 3a, c) show a typical three-stage strain-hardening behaviour for 6Al, with stages labelled A, D and E. Microhardness (Vickers) of the two phases in the Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C steels rises with Al content; the ferrite series begins at 6 wt% Al (the 6Al steel) at roughly 240–270 HV, and ferrite is significantly harder than austenite in all the designed steels, acting as the strengthening phase. The calculated stacking-fault energy of the 6Al austenite at 23 °C is 62.64 mJ m⁻², between the values for 4Al (51.25 mJ m⁻²) and 8Al (68.47 mJ m⁻²). Interrupted tensile tests were run to engineering strains of 3 %, 10 %, 20 % and 28 %. Characterisation techniques applied to this steel include SEM/EBSD (JSM-7800 F, 1 μm step size, HKL Channel 5), TEM (FEI Tecnai G2 F20 and FEI Talos F200X at 200 kV), SAED/two-beam analysis and DO3 dark-field imaging, HRTEM/IFFT, XRD, EPMA, wet-chemical analysis, Archimedes density measurement and MTS tensile testing with microhardness measurements.
summary: The 6Al steel is the austenite-matrix duplex member of a series of Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C (x = 4, 6, 8, 10 wt%) low-density steels, prepared by vacuum induction melting, homogenization at 1150 °C, hot forging and a terminal solution treatment at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by oil quenching. It consists of a quasi-equiaxed austenite matrix (97.0 % by mass) with 3.0 % ferrite located mainly at grain boundaries, contains L1_2-type short-range order in the austenite and coexisting B2/DO3 order in the ferrite, and combines a yield strength of 251 MPa with 51.6 % total elongation. It serves as the intermediate point in the paper's sequence describing how increasing Al converts an austenitic steel into a ferrite-based duplex steel.
unmapped: The 6Al steel mostly serves as the intermediate/reference member of the alloy series: the paper's detailed deformation-mechanism work — two-beam g·b analysis of dislocation types, dislocation pairing and DO3 shearing, dynamic slip band refinement (DSBR), multi-stage strain hardening stage analysis and flow-stress decomposition using the similitude coefficient K = 0.75 with σ0 = 455 MPa — was carried out on the 8Al and 10Al steels, not on the 6Al steel.

The 6Al steel's own deformed structure is documented in Fig. 4 panels (b, c): dense aligned dislocation bands in the austenite and straight parallel planar slip bands in the ferrite, the latter described in the citing text as less pronounced planar slip than in 8Al ferrite; the paper also notes that the complex planar slip of 10Al austenite at early deformation is similar to the 6Al steel reported in the authors' previous study.

The general duplex-steel interface stress-partitioning behaviour (high back/forward stresses at α/γ interfaces promoting collective glide and edge-dislocation activation, and the ~24.3 % soft austenite alleviating stress localisation in ferrite) is explicitly demonstrated on the 8Al steel and its ferrite–austenite boundaries, not on the 6Al steel.
16R/18R martensite and acicular precipitates are reported only for the 10Al steel (Mn- and C-enriched, Al-depleted), not for the 6Al steel.
